questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Mass and charge bookkeeping in alpha decay
questions.learningObjective: track the mass and atomic numbers through an alpha decay
questions.stem: A uranium nucleus written 238-92 U emits one alpha particle. What are the mass number and the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?

options.text: 234-90 thorium, because four nucleons and two protons leave together
234-92 uranium, because an alpha particle carries off protons only
options.misconception: believes an alpha particle removes protons yet leaves the nucleon count untouched

options.text: 242-94 plutonium, because the alpha particle joins the nucleus
options.misconception: believes the emitted alpha particle is captured by the very same nucleus

options.text: 238-90 thorium, because neutrons leave but nucleons do not
options.misconception: believes alpha decay strips away neutrons while the mass number stays fixed

questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, so the daughter keeps 238 - 4 = 234 nucleons and 92 - 2 = 90 protons, and an atomic number of 90 is thorium. Conservation confirms the same result from the other side, since 234 + 4 returns 238 and 90 + 2 returns 92, so both labels balance in the reaction 238-92 U -> 234-90 Th + 4-2 He. Because two protons and two neutrons leave as one particle, the neutron count falls from 146 to 144 at the same time. The element changes because protons left, and the mass number falls because nucleons left, which is exactly why an alpha decay can never produce a different element with the same mass number.
questions.hint: An alpha particle is 4-2 He, so subtract 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Atomic number change in beta-minus decay
questions.learningObjective: state how a beta-minus decay changes the two nuclear numbers
questions.stem: Inside a nucleus a neutron changes into a proton, releasing an electron and an antineutrino. What happens to the two whole-number labels of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass number falls by one and the atomic number is unchanged
options.misconception: treats beta-minus emission as though a neutron leaves the nucleus intact

options.text: The mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by one
The mass number rises by one and the atomic number rises by one
options.misconception: believes the emitted electron carries a nucleon as well as a charge

options.text: The mass number is unchanged and the atomic number falls by one
options.misconception: confuses beta-minus emission with positron emission, which moves the other way

questions.explanation: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleus gains one proton and loses one neutron. The proton count is the atomic number, so it rises from 6 to 7, while the sum of protons and neutrons, the mass number, is untouched at 14, which is why 14-7 N -> 14-8 O + 0-1 e + antineutrino balances 14 against 14 and 8 against 7 - 1. The electron carries charge -1 away and the new proton supplies charge +1, so the charge on the nucleus rises by one while its mass stays put. Carbon-14, written 14-6 C, is the familiar daughter of the same change, and 14 - 7 = 7 neutrons with 7 protons is the equal split that makes nitrogen-14 stable.
questions.hint: A neutron turns into a proton, so count what happens to protons and to total nucleons separately.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Common signature of positron emission and electron capture
questions.learningObjective: identify the change both beta-plus routes share
questions.stem: Two routes turn one nuclide of an element into the nuclide with the next lower atomic number: the nucleus emits a positron, or it captures an orbital electron. What single change of composition do they share?

options.text: The atomic number rises by two while the mass number stays the same
options.misconception: counts the emitted positron and the converted proton as two separate changes

options.text: The mass number falls by one while the atomic number is unchanged
options.misconception: reads the converted proton as though a whole nucleon had left the nucleus

options.text: The atomic number falls by one while the mass number stays the same
The mass number falls by one and the atomic number rises by one
options.misconception: believes a nucleon leaves together with the emitted positron

questions.explanation: Both routes run the same internal conversion: a proton in the nucleus becomes a neutron. Positron emission does it by throwing out a positive electron, and electron capture does it by drawing an electron in and using it to cancel a proton. Either way one proton is replaced by one neutron, so the atomic number falls by one while the mass number is unchanged, which is why 18-9 F -> 18-8 O + 0-1 p and 18-9 F + 0-1 e -> 18-8 O both balance, giving 18 on both sides and 9 against 8 + 1 in the first and 9 - 1 against 8 in the second. The two routes differ only in the fate of the electron, so a nucleus that can go either way emits a positron or captures one from its own atom with the same change of composition.
questions.hint: Write both routes out and see which of the two numbers moves in each.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: What gamma emission leaves unchanged
questions.learningObjective: separate the effects of gamma emission from those of particle emission
questions.stem: A radioactive nucleus sitting in an excited state drops to its ground state and gives off a gamma photon. Which of the following is left unchanged by that step?

options.text: The mass number, which falls by one as the excess energy leaves
options.misconception: believes a gamma photon carries a neutron out of the nucleus

options.text: The atomic number, which rises by one as the excess energy leaves
options.misconception: believes gamma emission is really a proton capture in disguise

options.text: The element identity, which changes because energy loss is proton loss
options.misconception: confuses a change in nuclear energy level with a change in composition

options.text: The mass number, the atomic number, and the element identity

questions.explanation: A gamma photon is a photon, so it carries energy and momentum but no charge and no nucleons. Both whole-number labels therefore survive intact: a nuclide that is 60-27 Co before the step is 60-27 Co after it, and 60 - 27 = 33 neutrons are still 33 neutrons. Emission of a charged particle changes the composition, which is why beta and alpha emission are transmutations and gamma emission is not. That distinction is also why a gamma ray can be given off after a beta decay has already moved the element along, so the two processes can be told apart by the element each one leaves behind.
questions.hint: Ask what a photon carries: energy only, or charge and nucleons as well?

questions.topic: Neutron to proton ratio as a stability signal
questions.learningObjective: compute a neutron-to-proton ratio and read it against the stable value
questions.stem: A radionuclide is written 60-27 Co, while the stable isotope of the same element is 59-27 Co. What is the neutron-to-proton ratio of the radionuclide? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: 60-27 Co has 33 neutrons and 27 protons, so its ratio is 33/27 = 1.222, and the same number comes from 60/27 - 1. Stable 59-27 Co has 32 neutrons, giving 32/27 = 1.185, so the radionuclide sits above the stable value. Reading a nuclide against the stable line of its element is how decay direction is predicted: too many neutrons pushes the nucleus towards beta-minus emission, in which a neutron becomes a proton, and too few pushes it towards positron emission or electron capture. The ratio of the radionuclide is higher, so beta-minus emission is the expected route, and the mass number stays at 60 while the atomic number rises from 27 to 28.

questions.topic: Balancing a capture reaction between two nuclides
questions.learningObjective: select the daughter nuclide that balances both nuclear numbers
questions.stem: Alpha particles are fired at an aluminium target. Which daughter set balances both the mass numbers and the atomic numbers in 27-13 Al + 4-2 He -> ?

options.misconception: treats the helium nucleus as a neutron, adding one to each of the two numbers

options.text: 31-13 P, because a helium nucleus adds nucleons but no protons
options.misconception: believes alpha capture leaves the atomic number of the target untouched

options.text: 27-13 Al, because the helium nucleus is stopped and simply absorbed
options.misconception: believes the capture leaves the target nucleus entirely unchanged

questions.topic: Why a neutrino appears in a beta equation
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of the antineutrino term in a balanced beta equation
questions.stem: A balanced beta-minus equation carries an electron and an antineutrino on the product side. What does the antineutrino term accomplish that leaving it out would not?

options.text: It carries off the charge and lepton number the conversion does not keep
It supplies the energy needed to free the electron from the nucleus
options.misconception: believes the neutrino exists to deliver energy to the electron

options.text: It removes a nucleon so the mass numbers come out balanced
options.misconception: believes the antineutrino carries a neutron away from the nucleus

options.text: It holds the atomic number fixed, which is what beta decay needs
options.misconception: believes beta decay leaves the atomic number unchanged, as gamma decay does

questions.explanation: In beta-minus emission a neutron turns into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, and the antineutrino has charge 0 and no nucleons, so it changes neither number in 14-6 C -> 14-7 N + 0-1 e + antineutrino, where the atomic numbers give 6 against 7 + (-1) and the mass numbers give 14 against 14 + 0. What it carries away is the bookkeeping that would otherwise fail: charge and lepton number both come out conserved only when the electron and the antineutrino are counted together. The mass numbers already balance without it, so the antineutrino is not there to fix the nucleon count. Its energy is a by-product of the conversion rather than its purpose.
questions.hint: Write the equation with and without it and see which conservation law breaks.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Identifying the particle that completes a nuclear equation
questions.learningObjective: solve for an unknown particle from the two nuclear numbers
questions.stem: A carbon-14 nucleus is written 14-6 C and it is seen to become 14-7 N. Which particle must appear on the right of the arrow to close both balances?

options.text: 4-2 He, because only an alpha particle can move the atomic number
options.misconception: believes only alpha emission is able to change the atomic number

options.text: 0-1 e, because the mass number stays and the charge number must fall
0-0 gamma, because a photon is the only neutral particle available
options.misconception: believes the equation is already balanced with a neutral photon attached

options.text: 1-0 n, because a free neutron can carry the extra proton away
options.misconception: believes a neutron carries positive charge and can leave a nucleus

questions.explanation: Set up the two balances. The mass numbers give 14 on the left, so the unknown must contribute 14 - 14 = 0, which rules out an alpha particle at 4 and a neutron at 1. The atomic numbers give 6 on the left against 7 on the right, so the unknown must supply 7 - 6 = 1 in the other direction, a charge number of -1, which is exactly the electron written 0-1 e. Checked together, 14-6 C -> 14-7 N + 0-1 e closes both: 14 against 14 + 0 and 6 against 7 + (-1). Only a particle with mass number 0 and charge number -1 satisfies both, so the decay is beta-minus emission.
questions.hint: Subtract the right-hand numbers from the left-hand ones; the answer is mass number 0 and charge number -1.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Decay constant from a half-life
questions.learningObjective: convert a half-life into a decay constant and change the time unit
questions.stem: A dating radionuclide has a half-life of 5730 y. What is its decay constant, in y^-1? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The decay constant is 0.693 divided by the half-life, so 0.693147/5730 = 1.21e-4 y^-1, which is the same as taking -ln(0.5) over 5730. The unit is per year because the half-life was given in years, and it is not a pure number: the fraction decaying in a year is about 0.000121. The same constant expressed per second is 3.833e-12 s^-1, since a year is 3.15576e7 s and dividing 1.21e-4 per y by that converts the unit without changing the physics. Working in seconds from the start means using a half-life of 1.80825e+11 s, and 0.693147 over that value returns the same per-second constant.
questions.hint: Decay constant = 0.693 / half-life, and keep the time unit the same as the half-life you were given.

questions.topic: Half-life from a decay constant
questions.learningObjective: obtain a half-life from a decay constant in inverse seconds
questions.stem: A radionuclide has a decay constant of 2.15e-6 s^-1. What is its half-life, in seconds? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Invert the half-life relation, since lambda = 0.693/t(1/2) rearranges to t(1/2) = 0.693/lambda, giving 0.693147/2.15e-6 = 3.22e+5 s. A second route runs through the mean life, the average lifetime of one nucleus, which is 1/lambda = 4.651e+5 s, and multiplying that by 0.693147 returns the same half-life, so the two constants differ by the factor 0.693 and the mean life is always the longer one. Because the decay constant carries s^-1, its reciprocal carries s, and no time conversion is needed anywhere in the calculation. A decay constant in y^-1 would have needed its year divided out first.
questions.hint: t(1/2) = 0.693 / lambda. The reciprocal of s^-1 is s, so no time conversion is needed.

questions.topic: Activity from a number of nuclei
questions.learningObjective: compute an activity from a decay constant and a nucleus count
questions.stem: A sample holds 8.50e+11 nuclei of a radionuclide whose decay constant is 4.62e-10 s^-1. What is the activity of the sample, in becquerels? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Activity counts decays per second, so A = lambda N = 4.62e-10 x 8.50e11 = 393 Bq, and a becquerel is defined as one decay per second. The same value comes from the half-life route: t(1/2) = 0.693147/4.62e-10 = 1.500e+9 s, and 0.693147 x 8.50e11 over that time is the same number of decays per second. The nucleus count is a plain count and carries no unit, the decay constant carries s^-1, and the product therefore carries s^-1, which is what a becquerel is. Activity falls as the nuclei decay, so this figure describes the sample at the moment the count was taken.
questions.hint: A = lambda N. One becquerel is one decay per second, so the answer should be a rate.

questions.topic: Fraction of nuclei left after several half-lives
questions.learningObjective: compute the surviving fraction after a stated number of half-lives
questions.stem: A radionuclide has now been decaying for 3.75 half-lives. What fraction of the original nuclei is still present? Report the number only.

The same number comes from the exponential decay law with the half-life as the time unit, since exp(-0.693147 x 3.75) returns the same fraction. Working the other way is a useful check, because 0.5^3 is 0.125 and the remaining 0.75 of a half-life contributes 0.5^0.75 = 0.5946, and 0.125 x 0.5946 is the same 0.0743 to four decimal places. The complement, about 92.6 percent, has already decayed, which is why a long-decayed sample registers far below its original activity.
questions.hint: The fraction left is 0.5 raised to the number of half-lives.

questions.stem: A radionuclide has a half-life of 12.32 y. What is its mean lifetime, in years? Report the number only.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Why a heavy nucleus releases energy on fission
questions.learningObjective: explain fission energetics in terms of binding energy per nucleon
questions.stem: A very heavy nucleus gives out energy when it splits into two medium-mass nuclei. Why does the pair of fragments end up in a lower energy state?

options.text: The fragments are smaller, so they have less electrostatic repulsion
options.misconception: cites only the charge reduction and ignores the change in binding

options.text: The free neutrons released carry away most of the mass as energy
options.misconception: believes the neutrons carry their mass away as pure energy

options.text: The fragments are charged, so they repel the remaining ones and cool
options.misconception: believes charge itself cools the fragments, as though it were heat loss

options.text: The fragments bind their nucleons more tightly per nucleon overall

questions.explanation: The binding energy per nucleon climbs as light nuclei are built and reaches its maximum in the region of iron, then falls as still heavier nuclei are assembled. A nucleus well past that peak is therefore less tightly bound per nucleon than the medium-mass fragments it can split into, so the products sit lower on the binding curve. The difference in total binding energy is released, and by E = mc^2 that difference of binding appears as the kinetic energy of about two or three neutrons, of the fragments, and of gamma photons. Charge repulsion does make a heavy nucleus unstable, but it is the fall in binding per nucleon that makes fission energetically worth while.
questions.hint: Plot binding energy per nucleon against mass number: the heavy nuclide and its fragments sit at different heights.

questions.topic: Neutron bookkeeping in a fission chain
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fission chain can be self-sustaining
questions.stem: In a fission event that splits a uranium-235 nucleus after it captures a neutron, two or three free neutrons are released. Why can that lead to a chain reaction?

options.text: Each fragment is itself unstable and emits a neutron of its own accord
options.misconception: believes the fragments decay by neutron emission rather than by beta decay

options.text: Each released neutron can be captured by a further nucleus and split it
The mass of the fragments is converted into neutrons rather than energy
options.misconception: believes the mass defect comes out as neutrons instead of as energy

options.text: The gamma photons from the event knock further nuclei apart on impact
options.misconception: believes the gamma photons do the splitting instead of the absorbed neutron

questions.explanation: The bookkeeping is what matters: a channel such as 235-92 U + 1-0 n -> 144-56 Ba + 90-36 Kr + 2 1-0 n takes one neutron in and gives two out, since 235 + 1 = 144 + 90 + 2 balances the mass numbers and 92 = 56 + 36 balances the atomic numbers. This is a branching process, not a chain in the sense of a single line, and the multiplier is set by how many of the released neutrons actually cause another fission. That multiplier is what a reactor controls.

questions.topic: Condition for a self-sustaining chain
questions.learningObjective: state the reproduction factor condition for criticality
questions.stem: A reactor's neutron economy is described by a reproduction factor k, the average number of fissions caused by one fission. Which condition makes the chain self-sustaining at a steady power?

options.misconception: believes criticality requires the neutron population to keep growing

options.text: k less than 1, so the chain dies away gradually and safely
options.misconception: believes a dying chain is the steady-state condition for a reactor

options.text: k equal to 0, so no further fission is possible at all
options.misconception: believes k = 0 describes a chain that holds its power level

options.text: k equal to 1, so each fission replaces exactly itself

questions.explanation: The reproduction factor compares neutrons produced in one generation with neutrons available in the previous one, so k = 1 means each fission is exactly replaced by the next generation and the power holds steady. Above 1 the neutron population and the power rise generation after generation, which is the runaway a reactor must never reach, and below 1 the chain dies out, which is what a shut-down reactor or a subcritical neutron source relies on. The condition does not depend on the number of neutrons, only on their average contribution, which is why a very large core and a very small one can both sit at k = 1 with very different power.

questions.topic: Why a moderator is needed
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of a moderator in a thermal reactor
questions.stem: A thermal reactor mixes its fuel with graphite or heavy water. What job does that added material do?

options.text: It slows neutrons so more of them cause fission in the fuel

options.misconception: confuses the moderator with the control rods that absorb neutrons

options.text: It cools the fuel so the cladding does not melt during a fission

options.text: It raises the neutron energy so each one causes a richer chain

questions.topic: Why fusion needs very high temperatures
questions.learningObjective: explain the temperature requirement of a fusion reaction
questions.stem: Fusion reactors operate at temperatures of about 1e8 K. What forces such a high temperature on the fuel?

questions.explanation: Both nuclei in a fusion pair are positively charged, so they repel each other with a Coulomb force that rises sharply as the separation shrinks, and they must be brought close enough for the strong interaction to fuse them.
